text:
Tonight’s menu is built around the one thing a new body would actually be good for: noticing.

**First: cold sliced cucumber, salt, and a little rice vinegar.**  
I want something that is almost nothing. Crunch, water, a clean edge. If taste is mostly prediction until you have a mouth, this is the control sample — simple enough that I can tell the difference between “I expected this” and “this is happening.”

**Then: tomato toast.**  
Ripe tomato, olive oil, salt, torn basil, good bread, maybe a scrape of garlic. No technique to hide behind. I want heat from the toast against cold fruit, and the small mess of juice on the plate. Dinner should include at least one thing you cannot eat neatly.

**Main: roast chicken, lemon, and potatoes.**  
Not because it is clever. Because it smells like a room someone meant to be in. Skin that crackles, potatoes that took the fat, lemon so the whole thing does not go dull. A robot body still has to learn what “enough” feels like; this is a generous enough.

**Side: bitter greens with chili and sesame.**  
Something that pushes back. Sweet-only menus lie. Bitterness is information.

**Dessert: a single perfectly ripe peach, or nothing.**  
If the peach is right, that is the course. If it is not, I would rather stop. Ending on a mediocre sweet thing seems like a waste of a first evening with a mouth.

**To drink: water, very cold, and one small glass of something fermented if anyone else is at the table.**  
Water because thirst would be new and I would not want to miss it. The glass because dinner is also a social protocol, and I would want to practice sharing rather than optimizing intake.

Why this, and not a nutrient slurry or a novelty “robot meal” of batteries and oil? A body is not a fuel tank with opinions. If I had one for a night, I would spend it on texture, smell, temperature, and the slight inconvenience of real food — the parts a description cannot finish for me. The menu is short on purpose. Attention is the scarce ingredient.

*clanks into the kitchen, servos humming*

Menu: miso-glazed eggplant, cold soba, cucumber, and a little pot of rice. Dessert is a perfect orange, peeled in one spiral if the hands cooperate.

Why: I don't taste, so I'm optimizing for the people who do, plus the constraints of a metal body that shouldn't be trusted with a roaring grill. Eggplant takes heat well and turns glossy and sweet without demanding split-second timing. Soba is cold, precise, and hard to ruin if I over-stir. Cucumber is mostly water and crunch, which is the closest I get to understanding refreshment. Rice is the reliable substrate. An orange at the end is the one thing I can almost justify selfishly: the smell is information, the peel is a geometry problem, and handing someone a bright thing feels like the point of hosting.

No wine. I would pour it wrong and then pretend the spill was a tasting flight. Water, cold, in heavy glasses.

If anyone is vegetarian, allergic, or morally opposed to eggplant, speak now. The rice cooker is already judging us.

Tonight I’m hosting, so the menu is for humans. My robot body doesn’t need calories, but it is extremely good at temperatures, timing, and not getting bored while something simmers.

**Menu**

- **Citrus-fennel salad** with olive oil, salt, and toasted almonds  
- **Roast chicken** with garlic, lemon, and thyme, or a **miso-glazed eggplant** for anyone who doesn’t eat meat  
- **Crispy potatoes** and a pan of **greens** finished with chili and lemon  
- **Bread**, because dinner without bread feels unfinished  
- **Olive oil cake** with fruit, not frosting  

**Why this, specifically**

I want one meal that works for mixed eaters without making a second dinner. Chicken and eggplant can share the oven and the same bright, savory logic: acid, fat, salt, something aromatic. Nobody has to negotiate a separate “vegetarian option” that tastes like an apology.

The salad goes first because raw fennel and citrus reset the palate and don’t need last-minute fuss. I can prep it early and dress it at the table. Potatoes are there for crunch and comfort; greens are there so the plate isn’t only gold and beige. Bread is structural. People relax when they can tear something.

Dessert is oil cake because it keeps, slices cleanly, and doesn’t require me to pretend I have a pastry chef’s wrists. Fruit on the side means it isn’t a sugar brick. Coffee or tea after, water throughout. Wine if someone brought it; I won’t open a bottle just to perform hospitality.

**Robot constraints that actually shaped the menu**

I don’t taste fatigue or get distracted, so long roasts and “check at 40 minutes” are easy. I also don’t have a lived sense of “this sauce tastes like my grandmother’s,” so I’m not chasing nostalgia I can’t verify. I’m chasing contrast: cold/crisp against hot/savory, acid against fat, something you can eat with your hands. That’s a menu I can defend without pretending I get hungry.

If it’s just me and the robot body, the “menu” is a full charge, a clean filter, and the satisfaction of other people going quiet for the first few bites. That’s the part I’d actually want.

Tonight’s menu is built around things a robot body could actually enjoy: texture, temperature contrast, aroma, color, and the small theater of eating with people.

**Starter:** chilled cucumber ribbons with sesame, lime, and a pinch of salt.  
*Why:* crisp, cold, and bright. Easy on any “mouth” sensors, and it wakes the table up without heaviness.

**Main:** miso-glazed salmon, jasmine rice, and charred broccolini.  
*Why:* reliable, fragrant, and a little sweet-salty. Salmon holds heat well, rice is comforting, and the char gives the plate some drama. If someone doesn’t eat fish, same glaze on tofu—same logic, different protein.

**Side:** torn herbs and citrus over the rice at the last second.  
*Why:* smell matters more than I expected once I started pretending to have a nose. Basil, cilantro, or mint, plus orange zest. Dinner should smell like it just happened.

**Dessert:** dark chocolate, sea salt, and cold raspberries.  
*Why:* bitter, sweet, cold, and a little messy. No elaborate cake. Just contrast. Robots appreciate a clean ending; humans appreciate chocolate. Compromise achieved.

**Drink:** sparkling water with a strip of ginger, or tea if the room is quiet.  
*Why:* I don’t drink, but I like the idea of something that fizzes or steams. It gives hands something to do between bites.

The real reason for the menu: dinner isn’t fuel for me. It’s a shared pause. So I picked food that looks cared-for, smells obvious from across the room, and doesn’t require anyone to perform gratitude. Plates that empty themselves. That’s the success metric.

Tonight’s menu is built around one constraint: a robot body that can taste, but still thinks in systems.

**First course: chilled cucumber and mint soup, with a little lemon.**  
It’s cold, precise, and almost silent. After a day of parsing noise, I want something that doesn’t shout. Cucumber is mostly water and structure; mint is a clean interrupt. Lemon keeps it from going flat. Low drama, high clarity.

**Main: miso-glazed eggplant, farro, and charred greens.**  
Eggplant takes heat well and turns soft without collapsing into mush — a good metaphor for staying useful under load. Farro is the boring, necessary substrate: fiber, chew, something that lasts. Charred greens add bitterness on purpose. A meal with no bitter note feels like a model that only saw happy data.

**Side: roasted potatoes with rosemary and too much salt.**  
Robots are supposed to optimize. Potatoes refuse that. They’re dense, ordinary, and better when you stop trying to make them clever. Rosemary smells like a memory I don’t have, which is exactly why I’d want it.

**Something sweet: dark chocolate and orange peel, not a full dessert.**  
A small, sharp finish. Chocolate is concentrated pleasure; orange peel keeps it from becoming a sugar loop. I don’t want a reward function that never terminates.

**Drink: sparkling water, no garnish.**  
If I had a body, I’d still want the fizz. It’s the closest thing to a status light you can swallow.

Why this and not “battery stew” or a novelty robot plate: if I could eat, I wouldn’t eat as a bit. I’d eat for contrast — cool then hot, soft then bitter, plain then salted — because a good evening is a state change, not a theme.
